title: The Doodles That Became a Brand
subtitle: A student noticed that the best notes often looked messy. Years later his branching diagrams were on BBC television — and the name “Mind Map” was a registered trademark.

card.essence: Put the topic in the middle of the page and let the ideas branch out from it — one keyword per line, with colour and pictures. You see the whole subject, and how its parts connect, at a glance.

intention: you'll learn where mind maps came from and what the evidence says about them, build one yourself, and practise phrasal verbs for ideas and notes: come up with, jot down, sum up, go over.
warmup: How do you take notes — in lines, lists, pictures, or not at all?
When you have to plan something big, how do you start?
Do you remember things better when you see them, hear them or write them down?

items.sent: Her desk was so cluttered that she couldn't find her keys.

vocab.heading: B · Which word matches the meaning?
vocab.intro: The three words are: hierarchy · keyword · branch. Read each meaning, say the word, then reveal.

items.sent: (noun) A line or part that grows out of a main part, like the arm of a tree.
items.meaning: branch — “Each branch of the map is a new subtopic.” (also: a local office of a bank or shop)

items.sent: (noun) One important word that reminds you of a whole idea.
items.meaning: keyword — “Write one keyword on each line, not a whole sentence.”

items.sent: (noun) A system in which things are arranged in levels of importance.
items.meaning: hierarchy — “The map shows a hierarchy: main ideas near the centre, details further out.” (adj. hierarchical)

vocab.heading: C · Which word completes all three phrases?
vocab.intro: One missing word fits every phrase in the group. Say it, then reveal.

items.meaning: spark — to make something start. (spark an idea / a debate / interest; noun a spark)

items.sent: a ___ of thought  ·  lose your ___ of thought  ·  a ___ of events
items.meaning: train — a connected series. (lose your train of thought = forget what you were going to say)
visual — connected with seeing. (visual memory, visual thinking, visual aids; verb visualise)

story.heading: Part 1 — Notes covered in mud
paras: Drawing ideas as branches is very old. In the third century, the philosopher Porphyry of Tyre showed Aristotle's categories as a branching diagram, and in the Middle Ages the thinker Ramon Llull used similar techniques.

Tony Buzan was born in 1942 in Palmers Green, north London, and moved with his family to Vancouver, Canada, when he was 12. Studying subjects including psychology, English and mathematics at the University of British Columbia, he noticed something odd. The students who did well did not necessarily have the neatest notes. Theirs were often messy — full of doodles, arrows and key words.
He began taking notes the same way. “It was as if I'd been driving all my life with my windscreen caked in mud,” he said later, “and suddenly I could see clearly.”
checks: Who drew Aristotle's categories as a branching diagram?
What did Buzan notice about the notes of successful students?
How did he describe the change in his own note-taking?
answers: Porphyry of Tyre, in the third century.
They were often messy, with doodles, arrows and key words — not neat.
Like driving with a windscreen covered in mud, and suddenly being able to see clearly.

story.heading: Part 2 — Use Your Head
paras: In the 1970s Buzan presented a BBC television series called Use Your Head, and in 1974 the BBC published a book of the same name. (Sources differ on whether the series began in 1973 or 1974.) It introduced viewers to his mind maps: one central idea in the middle of the page, main themes branching out from it, and details branching off those.

The rules were simple: start in the centre, use one keyword per line, use colour and pictures, and let the branches show how the ideas connect. His BBC books sold more than three million copies. He wrote around 80 books, and in 1991 he founded the World Memory Championships.
Buzan's organisation registered “Mind Maps” as a trademark, and in 2006 Buzan launched his own mind-mapping software, iMindMap. The doodles had become a brand.
checks: What was the name of Buzan's BBC series?
What are the basic rules of a mind map?
What did Buzan's organisation do with the name?
answers: Start in the centre, one keyword per line, use colour and pictures, show the connections with branches.
It registered “Mind Maps” as a trademark.
story.discuss: Should anyone be able to own the name of a way of thinking?

story.heading: Part 3 — Genius or salesman?
paras: Buzan was a showman, and not everyone was convinced. His obituary in The Times noted that some people thought him “little more than a good salesman”. Critics also pointed out that branching diagrams were centuries older than Buzan.

So what does the research say? In a 2002 study of 50 medical students in London, the group taught to use mind maps remembered about 10% more of a text a week later than a group using their own study methods — a modest gain, and not a certain one. The mind-map group was also less motivated to use the technique.

Buzan died in April 2019. Mind maps did not turn ordinary people into geniuses, as some of the advertising suggested. But for planning a project, an essay or a wedding, a single page that shows the whole picture can still be surprisingly useful.
checks: What did some people think of Buzan, according to The Times?
What was the problem with motivation?
answers: That he was “little more than a good salesman”.
The mind-map group remembered about 10% more after a week — a modest, uncertain gain.
The students using mind maps were less motivated to use the technique.
story.discuss: Why do you think some people love mind maps and others can't stand them?

tool_tab.lead: The topic goes in the middle. Main ideas branch out from it; details branch off the main ideas. The further from the centre, the more specific the idea.
how: Turn the page sideways and write the topic in the centre — with a picture if you can.
Draw thick lines for the main ideas, one keyword on each.
Add thinner branches for details. Jump around freely; there's no right order.
Look for connections between branches and draw arrows — this is often where the best ideas appear.

sort.intro: A couple are mind-mapping their wedding. Where does each item go: the centre, a main branch, or a sub-branch?

items.why: one of the big themes of the plan.
a detail of the Venue branch.
the topic of the whole map.
a detail of the Food branch.
a detail of a Guests branch.

breaks: Pretty isn't the same as clear. It's easy to spend more time on colours than on thinking.
One centre only. Problems with several equally important parts don't fit a single middle point.
Hard to share. A map that makes perfect sense to you can be a mystery to everyone else.
discuss: Make a quick mind map of your next week. What did you notice that a list would have hidden?
When would you choose a list instead of a mind map?

grammar.name: phrasal verbs for ideas and notes
grammar.lead: When people talk about ideas and notes, they use a lot of phrasal verbs: come up with an idea, jot down a word, sum up a meeting. The tricky part is where the object goes.
notes:
Phrasal verbs = verb + particle (up, down, out, over…). The meaning often isn't obvious from the parts.
“jot down” = write quickly  “sum up” = summarise  “go over” = review  “leave out” = omit  “branch out” = move into new areas

Separable verbs: a noun object can go before or after the particle.
“Write down the word.” = “Write the word down.”

Inseparable verbs: the object always comes after the particle.
“She came across an old notebook.” (= found it by chance)  “Look at the centre.”

Three-part verbs keep all their parts together.
“come up with a plan”  “run out of space”  “keep up with the lecture”
Watch out: with separable verbs, a pronoun must go in the middle: ~~Write down it~~ → “Write it down.” ~~Sum up them~~ → “Sum them up.”

exercises.heading: Choose the phrasal verb
exercises.intro: Complete each sentence with the correct form of: come up with, jot down, sum up, run out of, go over.
items: 1. Can you ___ the main points in one sentence?
2. We need to ___ a name for the new product by Friday.
3. I always ___ my notes the night before an exam.
4. She ___ the phone number on the back of an envelope.
5. Halfway through the meeting, my pen ___ ink.

exercises.heading: Where does the pronoun go?
exercises.intro: Rewrite each sentence, replacing the words in bold with it or them.
items: 2. She came across the old notebook in a drawer. → ___
answers: 2. She came across it in a drawer. (inseparable)

grammar.closing: Now tell your teacher how you prepare for something important — a trip, an exam, a presentation — using at least four phrasal verbs from today.

speak.intro: Think in branches, out loud. Choose a task, start the timer, and talk.
speak.useful: “In the middle, I'd put …” · “One main branch is …” · “That links to …” · “Let me jot that down.” · “To sum up, …”

tasks.label: Task 1 — Map it
paras: Choose a topic — your job, your town, a hobby. Describe the mind map you would draw: the centre, four main branches and some details.

tasks.label: Task 2 — Your notes
paras: Describe how you take notes at work, in class or on your phone. Has your method changed over the years? Why?

tasks.label: Task 3 — Genius or salesman?
paras: Buzan was admired and criticised. Talk about another person who sold a simple idea very successfully. Did they deserve their success?

final: Is a method less valuable if someone makes a lot of money from it?
Why do people trust a technique more when it comes with an exciting story?
Should schools teach note-taking as a skill? How?
